title: RO pretreatment for pharmaceutical water systems | Aquemi
meta: Pretreatment that takes drinking water meeting USP <1231> and holds RO feed at no detectable chlorine or chloramine and SDI ≤ 3, in every Canadian season.
eyebrow: PRETREATMENT · USP <1231> · HEALTH CANADA · US EPA NPDWR
headline: Pretreatment that keeps chlorine, chloramine and scale off reverse osmosis membranes, every season
lead: Drinking water is not reverse osmosis (RO) feed. We design from your seasonal water data, so the RO inlet sees no detectable chlorine or chloramine and a silt density index (SDI) of 3 or less.

blocks.h: Canadian feed water and what it does
blocks.intro: Season and source change the water; each condition sets part of the design.
rows: Chloramine, used by many large utilities
Oxidizes polyamide membranes, reacts slowly on carbon, and releases ammonia that can reach the electrodeionization (EDI) unit.
Catalytic carbon, two beds or bisulfite; total chlorine at the RO inlet; ammonia strategy agreed with the Purified Water (PW) skid.
Winter near 2 °C, summer over 20 °C
Cold cuts RO output and silica and calcium solubility. Warm water speeds growth in carbon and softeners.
Membranes sized at your coldest month or a feed heat exchanger; sanitization frequency set for summer.
Spring runoff and fall turnover
Turbidity and organics raise SDI and total organic carbon (TOC), foul membranes and load the carbon.
Media filter sized for the worst month, SDI tested on site, ultrafiltration where media cannot hold SDI.
Hardness and alkalinity, highest in groundwater
Calcium carbonate scales the last elements. Alkalinity becomes CO₂ that loads the EDI.
Duplex softeners regenerated on measured hardness; concentrate LSI checked; CO₂ handed to the PW skid.
Silica
Passes softeners, scales the concentrate, limits recovery and loads the EDI and any still.
Recovery limited at your coldest feed; antiscalant where projections need it.
Iron and manganese, mostly well water
Foul membranes and coat resin at levels drinking water allows.
Oxidation and catalytic media ahead of the softener, sized on more than one season.
No disinfectant after carbon
Biofilm in carbon and softeners sheds into the RO and raises PW bioburden.
Hot water sanitizable carbon, samples around each bed, flow at no demand.

blocks.h: Questions validation and engineering teams ask

items.q: Our water meets drinking water standards. Why is that not enough?
items.a: Those standards are set for health and taste. The US EPA National Primary Drinking Water Regulations (NPDWR) allow chloramine up to 4 mg/L as Cl₂, and Health Canada sets no chloramine limit. Polyamide membranes are typically rated for less than 0.1 mg/L free chlorine, and a few mg/L of calcium scales the concentrate.

items.q: Do we have to prove our feed water meets drinking water standards?
items.a: The USP and Ph. Eur. monographs make PW from drinking water, and USP <1231> names it as the minimum source quality, so an auditor will expect evidence. For municipal supply: utility reports plus your own periodic tests at the plant inlet. For a well, a sampling programme against the Canadian guidelines or the NPDWR, including microbiology.

items.q: How do you show the design covers seasonal swings before we order?
items.a: We ask for [months of history] of utility and site data, find the worst month for each parameter and size every bed against it. Utilities report turbidity, not SDI, so we test SDI on site where we can, and again at SAT. You see the design basis, month by month, before you order.

items.q: Is pretreatment part of the validated system?
items.a: Your risk assessment draws that boundary; many sites qualify from the RO inlet onward. Either way it is in the turnover package, tested at FAT and SAT, and documented to the same standard, with installation and operational qualification (IQ/OQ) protocols where you bring it into scope.

items.q: Our municipality uses chloramine. Is standard carbon enough?
items.a: Usually not at a reasonable bed size: chloramine reacts slowly on carbon, slower in cold water. We use catalytic carbon, two beds in series or bisulfite, and alarm on total chlorine, because a free chlorine analyser does not see chloramine. If your utility switches to free chlorine for a few weeks a year, we design for both.

items.q: What happens to the ammonia from chloramine?
items.a: RO rejects it well as ammonium, but at the higher pH used to control CO₂ more of it is ammonia gas, which passes the membrane and loads the EDI. So chloramine removal here and the CO₂ strategy on the PW skid are designed together. See Purified Water generation.

items.q: Can we keep our existing pretreatment when we replace the RO?
items.a: Often, if it meets the new RO inlet targets. We review its sizing, media age, sanitization and monitoring against your feed data, and tell you what to keep, upgrade or replace. See upgrades and retrofits.

items.q: Who changes media, resin and cartridges after handover?
items.a: Our service team, from [service locations], with a severity 1 on-site response of [severity 1 on-site response time, hours]. Media, resin and cartridges for your train are stocked in [stocking location], and every visit ends with a signed report your quality unit can file.
